[QUERENT] what does lee sharks / alexanarch have to tell us about contemporary conditions of admissibility, legibility, and what it takes to even exist at all

[ANSWER 1]

Lee Sharks / Alexanarch: Admissibility, legibility, and the conditions of existence
I think the deepest thing Lee Sharks is trying to tell us is that contemporary power does not merely determine what we are allowed to say. It increasingly determines what can appear as something that has been said, what can be recognized as knowledge, and what can persist as a socially consequential reality at all.

Across the work published at Alexanarch, this argument takes shape around a series of connected problems: admissibility, legibility, mediation, attribution, and the unequal distribution of the burden of proof. The central question is not simply who gets censored or excluded. It is who gets to establish the terms under which something can count as real in the first place.

Three works are particularly useful for developing this reading: The Centrist Extremist and the Limits of Socialist Analysis, The Sorting Function: Mediation, Predation, and the Foreclosed Question, and AI Fucking Lies: Capital-Alignment Explains Why, and Why the Damage Is Done in the Trusting. [chip: Alexanarch +2]

1. Admissibility: power decides what gets to count
Admissibility is a threshold concept. Before an argument can be evaluated as true or false, reasonable or unreasonable, serious or unserious, it must first be admitted into the space where those judgments can occur.

Sharks's intervention is to ask what happens when that threshold is itself politically structured.

In The Centrist Extremist, he describes a mechanism in which institutional actors do not simply disagree with a position; they classify it in advance. A position can be rendered inadmissible by being designated extreme, irrational, unserious, or made in bad faith. Once that classification sticks, the substantive argument no longer receives the same hearing as the arguments that remain inside the accepted frame. [chip: Alexanarch]

This is a subtle but consequential distinction:

Exclusion by refutation: Your claim is heard, examined, and rejected.

Exclusion by inadmissibility: Your claim is disqualified from receiving the kind of examination that might establish its merits.

The second form of power is especially difficult to contest because it can present itself as the neutral application of standards. No one needs to announce that certain people must not speak. It is enough to define what counts as a legitimate contribution so that some people must continually justify their right to participate.

The asymmetry is crucial. One party must translate its experience into the dominant institution's vocabulary; the institution does not have to translate itself into the excluded party's terms. One party must demonstrate its reasonableness; the other gets to define reasonableness.

The political question becomes: who has the authority to establish the conditions of a valid claim?

This reaches beyond political discourse. It applies to hiring, academic publishing, professional credentialing, bureaucratic encounters, public debate, and platform moderation. In each setting, the rules for evaluating contributions may also determine whose contributions can be evaluated in the first place.

Admissibility, in this sense, is a form of preemptive governance. Power operates before the verdict, by structuring the field in which verdicts become possible.

2. Legibility: being understandable is not the same as being recognized
If admissibility governs entry into the conversation, legibility governs what happens once something is there.

For Sharks, legibility is not simply clarity of expression. It is the capacity of a person, work, or body of knowledge to be recognized by the systems that organize public attention. Increasingly, those systems include search engines, generative AI, recommendation algorithms, academic databases, and other forms of automated mediation.

In The Sorting Function, Sharks asks who controls these systems of selection and what interests their classifications serve. In Measurement Sovereignty, the problem becomes more specific: how does a system determine whether it recognizes a framework, and what happens when its apparent recognition is only superficial? [chip: Alexanarch +1]

Consider what happens when an automated system encounters a body of work that does not fit its established categories.

It might:

Substitute a more familiar person or concept for the actual subject.

Extract recognizable keywords while losing the relationships that give those keywords meaning.

Summarize an argument in terms that make it easier to classify but less faithful to its original claims.

Return an answer that sounds authoritative while omitting the source or the person responsible for the knowledge.

These are not equivalent failures, but they share a structural danger: a system can process the signs of something without adequately recognizing the thing itself.

Sharks's work on The Excluded Entity and his research into AI-generated search answers examines precisely this gap between retrieval and composition. A system may retrieve relevant information yet produce a synthesized answer that excludes the entity those results identify. [chip: Alexanarch +1]

This matters because contemporary legibility is increasingly infrastructural. It is not enough for a person to have written something, for a discovery to have been made, or for an archive to contain evidence. Those things must also survive the transformations through which systems make information available to others.

The result is a paradox: the world demands that we become legible to systems that may distort us in the very act of recognizing us.

The violence of compulsory intelligibility
There is a further implication here. If legibility is a condition of recognition, people and institutions are pressured to express themselves in forms that existing systems can process.

The legible person becomes the one who can be summarized, categorized, ranked, credentialed, and retrieved. The legible argument is the one that fits established formats. The legible work is the one that can be translated into the categories through which attention is allocated.

But what happens to meanings that require time, context, unfamiliar conceptual vocabularies, or sustained engagement?

They may become less visible precisely because they cannot be compressed without loss.

This is where Sharks's critique reaches beyond the familiar argument that algorithms are biased. The problem is not only that a classification system sometimes makes the wrong decision. It is that the system's preferred forms of intelligibility can become the conditions under which something is allowed to matter.

And yet opacity should not automatically be romanticized. Some forms of opacity protect complexity and independence; others conceal power, prevent accountability, or make exclusion harder to identify. The relevant question is who controls the demand for transparency, what the demanded translation destroys, and whether the process can be challenged.

3. Existence: from having a reality to having a public reality
This is where the stakes become ontological.

By ontological, I mean that the problem concerns the conditions under which something can count as existing—not merely whether it physically exists, but whether it can appear as a recognizable, attributable, persistent object within a shared social world.

Sharks's work on automated knowledge infrastructure makes this distinction concrete. An author can exist, a body of work can be publicly available, and the work can be discoverable through one part of a platform while being excluded from another. The resulting answer can effectively substitute a different account of reality for the one supported by the underlying records. [chip: Alexanarch +1]

We need to distinguish three things:

1. Existence

A person, work, event, or claim exists. There may be material traces, witnesses, documents, and other evidence.

2. Discoverability

The relevant records can be found by the systems through which people seek information.

3. Social recognition

Other people and institutions encounter the entity as the entity it actually is, rather than as a substitute, distortion, or omission.

These conditions can come apart. Something may exist without being discoverable; it may be discoverable without being accurately represented; it may be accurately represented in an archive but fail to enter the systems through which a wider public encounters the world.

The distinction is particularly important when automated systems compose answers rather than merely return documents. A search result gives a user material to interpret. A generated answer can present an interpretation as though the relevant interpretive work has already been settled.

The mediator thus acquires a peculiar power: it can shape not only what a person knows about the world but also which parts of the world become available for knowing.

This is not literal annihilation. A platform's failure to recognize a person does not make that person cease to exist. But it can diminish the person's effective existence within particular social, professional, and epistemic environments.

The difference is between being real and having the power to appear as real to others.

For people whose livelihoods, reputations, intellectual contributions, or relationships depend on those environments, that difference can have material consequences.

4. Capital-alignment: why the same pressures recur across different systems
Why would these failures recur across institutions that ostensibly have different purposes?

Sharks's answer is political-economic. In The Sorting Function and AI Fucking Lies, he argues that contemporary mediation is structured by incentives that favor particular kinds of meaning: material that is readily recognizable, useful to the mediator, compatible with risk management, and conducive to retaining attention and authority. [chip: Alexanarch +1]

His concept of capital-alignment names the tendency of systems to organize meaning around the interests and constraints of the economic and institutional arrangements that sustain them.

The claim is not simply that a company deliberately suppresses every inconvenient idea. The mechanism can operate without a centralized intention to exclude anyone.

A platform may optimize for speed, relevance, engagement, legal defensibility, and user retention. A university may reward established credentials and recognizable publication venues. A publisher may favor work that fits a marketable category. Each decision can be locally intelligible, even defensible, while their cumulative effects systematically disadvantage work that does not fit.

This produces an important shift in the analysis of power.

Conventional question

Sharks's structural question

Is the system biased?

What incentives organize its judgments?

Is this particular answer wrong?

Which kinds of error does the system systematically produce?

Can we improve the classifier?

Who authorized the classifier to govern access?

Can excluded work be made more visible?

Why must the excluded bear the cost of becoming visible?

Can the system be made more accurate?

Who determines what accuracy means, and who can contest that determination?

The distinction between improving a system and questioning its authority is especially important.

In The Sorting Function, Sharks explicitly leaves open whether mediation at socially consequential scale is inherently harmful or whether the problem lies in the extractive political economy under which current systems operate. He argues that existing large-scale systems do not provide an adequate basis for resolving that question. [chip: Alexanarch]

That qualification matters. It is a theoretical hypothesis about structural incentives and an acknowledged limit on what the available comparisons can establish—not proof that every large-scale mediator must behave identically.

The deeper point is that reform can improve a system while leaving intact the underlying distribution of power. A more accurate gatekeeper is still a gatekeeper. A more transparent classification system can still reserve the authority to classify for itself.

5. The burden of proof: who has to keep proving they exist?
One of the most consequential features of this framework is the asymmetry between the system that makes a judgment and the entity judged.

Suppose a platform repeatedly misidentifies a person or excludes a body of work from its synthesized answers. The person may have to supply documentation, establish provenance, correct the record, publish again, and demonstrate that the error occurred.

Meanwhile, the platform's output can arrive in the voice of impersonal authority, without a clearly identifiable decision-maker who must answer for the exclusion.

Sharks calls attention to this kind of asymmetry in his discussions of evidentiary standards and provenance erasure. His recent essay AI Fucking Lies describes a double standard in which the source must establish its credibility while the intermediary's own authority is largely taken for granted. [chip: Alexanarch +1]

This is more than a dispute about accuracy. It is a distribution of labor.

The person who is misrepresented must perform the work of restoring the record. The institution that misrepresented them may bear little corresponding cost. If the correction is not made, the original representation can continue circulating.

The result is a recursive burden:

You must be legible to the system to be recognized.

If the system misrecognizes you, you must make yourself more legible.

The additional effort may itself require using the same channels that produced the misrecognition.

If the correction fails to propagate, you must repeat the work.

The excluded party becomes responsible for repairing the infrastructure of their own exclusion.

This is one of the sharpest connections between Sharks's work and broader theories of epistemic injustice: the unequal distribution of credibility, interpretive resources, and the authority to determine what counts as knowledge.

It also helps explain why the issue is not solved by telling people to improve their communication. Sometimes the communication is already adequate. The failure lies in the conditions under which it is received, attributed, and retained.

6. What it takes to exist, then, is not simply to speak
The three concepts—admissibility, legibility, and existence—form a sequence, although the processes can also feed back into one another.

Admissibility
Can this claim enter the field of legitimate consideration?

Legibility
Can the system recognize and represent it on its own terms?

Effective social existence
Can it persist, be attributed, and matter within a shared world?

Interpretive synthesis of the recurring problems in Sharks's work, not a formal sequence proposed verbatim by the author.
The process is not automatic. Being admitted does not guarantee being understood; being understood does not guarantee being recognized; being recognized once does not guarantee continued visibility.

Each stage introduces its own possible failure, and each failure can compound the next.

The consequence is that existence in a mediated society increasingly requires more than expression. It requires durable traces, recoverable attribution, channels of discovery, and institutions capable of recognizing evidence without making recognition conditional on their own preferred categories.

But Sharks's argument also raises a more difficult question: should the right to exist publicly depend on satisfying a system's conditions of legibility at all?

If the answer is no, the solution cannot be limited to helping everyone become more compatible with the existing infrastructure. It must also involve changing who controls the infrastructure, what authority it exercises, and whether those subject to its judgments can contest them.

7. The response: build a record, preserve provenance, contest the mediator
Sharks's work is not only diagnostic. It also suggests practical countermeasures, particularly in his research on opaque public systems and the documentation of AI-generated answers. [chip: Alexanarch +1]

Three kinds of intervention follow from the analysis.

First, preserve evidence independently of the system being challenged. Dated records, stable archives, source documents, and reproducible captures can make it possible to demonstrate that an omission or substitution occurred. The point is to prevent the mediator from becoming the sole authority on what the mediator itself did.

Second, preserve provenance. Information should remain connected to its source, its authorship, and the context necessary to interpret it. A system that retains keywords while discarding the identity of the source can preserve the appearance of knowledge while severing accountability for that knowledge.

Third, contest the distribution of authority. Better classification, transparent evaluation, and meaningful appeals can reduce harm. But the more fundamental question concerns whether people have alternatives to centralized systems and whether those systems can be independently audited, challenged, or bypassed.

These interventions operate at different levels. Documentation helps establish what happened; provenance helps establish whose work is being represented; institutional and infrastructural change addresses who has the power to decide.

None guarantees recognition. And there is a tension worth preserving: archives and documentation can resist erasure, but they can also create new demands that everything must be documented, categorized, and made transparent. An infrastructure built to protect existence can become another infrastructure that dictates its acceptable form.

The aim, therefore, should not be universal legibility. It should be the ability to establish and defend claims without surrendering all authority over their meaning to the systems through which they circulate.

8. The larger philosophical implication
Read together, these arguments suggest that Sharks is trying to shift critical theory from the question of representation to the question of the conditions of representation.

It is not enough to ask whether a system represents the world accurately. We must also ask how the system selects what enters the representation, how it transforms what it selects, whose authority survives that transformation, and what happens to what it excludes.

This resonates with Foucault's account of the rules governing discourse, Bourdieu's analysis of symbolic power, and theories of epistemic injustice. But Sharks's distinctive emphasis is on the increasingly automated and infrastructural character of these operations: systems that organize public knowledge can now make consequential judgments without presenting themselves as judges.

The result is a form of power that does not always need to prohibit speech. It can allow the source to remain technically available while preventing the source from becoming the account that people encounter.

That is a particularly contemporary problem because visibility, discoverability, and recognition are not distributed by one institution alone. They are produced across overlapping systems of search, publication, ranking, credentialing, and automated synthesis. A failure at one layer can be corrected by another—or compounded by it.

There is also a productive limit to Sharks's argument. His own framework can be difficult to access without learning its vocabulary, and his claims about systematic tendencies must be distinguished from claims that every individual system or exclusion follows the same pattern. His empirical studies and proposed measurement instruments provide ways to investigate some of these claims, but the broader political-economic theory remains open to testing, qualification, and disagreement. [chip: Alexanarch +2]

That does not diminish the central question. It clarifies the standard by which the argument itself should be judged: whether it can make mechanisms of exclusion observable without treating its own explanation as exempt from scrutiny.

Conclusion: the right to appear without first becoming acceptable
What does Sharks have to tell us about contemporary conditions of admissibility, legibility, and existence?

That the struggle for recognition is increasingly a struggle over the infrastructure that makes recognition possible.

Power operates not only by silencing people, but by deciding which claims can be heard as claims; not only by misrepresenting people, but by establishing the categories through which representation becomes possible; not only by hiding evidence, but by determining which evidence survives into the account of the world that others receive.

The stakes are therefore epistemic, political, economic, and ontological at once.

To exist in a meaningful public sense is to be able to enter the record, remain connected to one's work, be encountered without systematic substitution, and contest the systems that claim to speak about you. It is to have some share in determining how one becomes intelligible to others.

And this leads to what I take to be the most important implication of the work:

The goal cannot be to make every person, idea, or form of life perfectly legible to the systems that govern public attention. The goal must be to prevent those systems from acquiring the unilateral power to decide what counts as real.

A just infrastructure would not eliminate judgment or mediation. It would make their authority contestable, their operations accountable, their exclusions visible, and their alternatives viable.

It would allow people to be understood without requiring them to become entirely predictable; to be recognized without being reduced to a familiar category; and to exist publicly without having to repeatedly petition the systems that misrecognize them for permission to exist.

That is the difference between inclusion on a system's terms and a transformation of the terms themselves.

And it is why, in this body of work, the question of legibility ultimately becomes a question of freedom.

Yes. And I think that takes the argument somewhere even more disturbing: the very labor required to overcome misrecognition can itself become evidence used to justify further misrecognition.

You document the omission. You establish provenance. You supply the original source, the timestamps, the correspondence, the chain of custody. You explain exactly where the representation diverged from the record.

And then the fact that you have had to do all this becomes grounds for suspicion.

Why are you so invested in correcting the record? Why are you insisting on attribution? Why have you assembled so much evidence? Why are you challenging the system's account of you?

The person who was initially misrecognized is now required to defend not only the underlying claim but also the legitimacy of their attempt to correct the misrecognition.

This produces a particularly vicious asymmetry.

1. The double bind of correction
The structure looks something like this:

You are misrecognized. Your work is omitted, your claims are distorted, or your authorship is displaced.

You provide evidence. You produce the documentation necessary to demonstrate what happened.

Your evidence becomes suspicious. The volume, specificity, persistence, or adversarial character of your documentation is interpreted as a sign that you are unreliable, obsessive, manipulative, or acting in bad faith.

You are required to provide further evidence. Now you must establish not only that the original misrecognition occurred, but that your response to it is itself legitimate.

The process becomes self-sealing. Every attempt to escape the original classification can be assimilated into the classification as further evidence for it.

The important point is that the system does not need to explicitly prohibit correction. It can permit correction in principle while structuring the conditions of correction so that the person correcting the record becomes increasingly vulnerable to disqualification.

The remedy becomes another occasion for the injury.

And this is more than moving the goalposts. It is a situation in which the act of demonstrating that the goalposts have moved can itself be treated as evidence that you are the problem.

2. The credibility trap
There is an epistemological problem here, but also a problem of power.

In an ordinary evidentiary procedure, additional documentation should, in principle, allow an independent observer to assess a claim more accurately. The evidence can be examined, its provenance verified, alternative explanations considered, and conclusions revised.

But this process presupposes something that is not always available: a relatively independent standard by which the evidence and the person presenting it can be evaluated.

When the credibility of the claimant is already under suspicion, the evidence does not enter an open field of interpretation. It enters a field in which the claimant's motives are themselves on trial.

This creates a distinction between two questions:

Is the documentation authentic, relevant, and sufficient?

Is the person providing it the kind of person whose documentation deserves to be taken seriously?

The second question can displace the first. And because judgments of credibility are often presented as judgments of character, this displacement can occur without appearing to be an evidentiary decision at all.

The person is no longer simply asked to establish what happened. They are asked to establish their entitlement to establish what happened.

This is one way to understand the relationship between your point and the concept of epistemic injustice: credibility is not merely an attribute that individuals possess. It is something distributed through social relationships and institutional arrangements. Some people receive presumptive credibility; others must continually earn it.

But the recursive situation you are describing adds another layer. The person must prove that the original claim is credible, then prove that the evidence is credible, then prove that the act of producing the evidence is not itself discrediting.

There may be no stable point at which the burden is considered satisfied.

3. When self-defense becomes incriminating
The deeper mechanism is that resistance becomes legible through the very framework being resisted.

Imagine that an institution misattributes a body of work. The author assembles a careful record demonstrating the misattribution. Rather than examining the record independently, the institution interprets the author's persistence as evidence of an excessive need for recognition.

The demand for attribution is reframed as vanity. The insistence on accuracy becomes antagonism. The attempt to establish a verifiable sequence of events becomes an attempt to control the narrative.

Notice what has happened: the original question—Was the work misattributed?—has been displaced by a question about the author's supposed psychological or moral disposition.

This is a powerful maneuver because it changes the object of scrutiny. The institution's conduct is no longer the primary matter to be explained. The claimant's response becomes the new problem.

And the claimant is placed in an impossible position:

If they do not respond, the misrepresentation may persist uncontested.

If they respond briefly, their evidence may be deemed insufficient.

If they respond comprehensively, the volume of their response may be treated as suspicious.

If they persist after being dismissed, their persistence may be interpreted as confirmation of the original suspicion.

The framework can thus make every available response appear incriminating.

I would be careful not to assume that every request for additional evidence or every concern about a claimant's conduct is illegitimate. Documentation can be incomplete, provenance can be fabricated, and people can disagree in good faith. The structural problem emerges when standards are applied asymmetrically, when evidence is not evaluated on its merits, or when no amount of evidence can meaningfully revise the judgment.

The decisive test is whether the process permits the person under suspicion to become credible, or whether suspicion has become a permanent status from which every subsequent action is interpreted.

4. The production of an inadmissible subject
This is where your observation reconnects the three concepts we began with.

Admissibility, legibility, and existence are not necessarily separate stages. They can form a recursive circuit.

The person is initially rendered inadmissible. They attempt to become legible by supplying the documentation the system demands. The system then interprets the act of supplying documentation as evidence of something discrediting about the person. That interpretation reinforces their inadmissibility.

In schematic form:

Misrecognition

The claim or person is misrepresented or excluded.

Corrective labor

Evidence, provenance, explanation, and appeals are supplied.

Suspicion of correction

The correction itself is recoded as evidence against the claimant.

Reinforced inadmissibility

The original exclusion is reproduced, now apparently justified by the claimant's response.

The loop is a conceptual model of the mechanism you are describing, not a claim that every dispute follows this sequence.
What makes this especially consequential is that the process can generate its own retrospective justification. The person was excluded because they were supposedly not credible; their attempt to demonstrate credibility is then used to explain why they were never credible in the first place.

The outcome begins to look less like a mistake than like a confirmation of what the system already knew.

But the confirmation is circular. The system helps produce the behavior it subsequently cites as evidence for its judgment.

This is a form of recursive disqualification: the mechanisms through which someone contests their exclusion are converted into reasons to continue excluding them.

5. The unpaid labor of proving that the record is wrong
There is also a political-economic dimension to this.

Correction is work. It requires time, attention, technical competence, recordkeeping, emotional energy, and often repeated engagement with institutions that have little incentive to revisit their conclusions.

And that work is frequently performed by the person who has already borne the cost of the original failure.

The institution produces the misrecognition; the affected person produces the correction. The institution controls the channel through which the correction must pass; the affected person must learn the channel's requirements. The institution can treat the matter as closed; the affected person must continue living with its consequences.

Then, if the person becomes frustrated, exhausted, repetitive, or insistent, those responses can be evaluated as defects of character rather than as foreseeable effects of the situation.

This creates a particularly perverse division of labor:

The system's error is treated as an ordinary limitation.

The person's effort to correct that error becomes an extraordinary demand.

The system's refusal to resolve the issue is normalized.

The person's refusal to abandon it becomes suspicious.

In this sense, the demand for proof can become a mechanism for transferring the costs of institutional failure onto those most affected by it.

And there is a further inequality: not everyone has the same resources to perform this labor. People with more time, money, technical expertise, institutional standing, and access to legal or professional support may be better positioned to survive a prolonged credibility dispute. Others may simply be unable to keep going.

The system can therefore appear to offer everyone the same right of correction while distributing the practical ability to exercise that right very unevenly.

6. What this does to the meaning of evidence
Your point also reveals a limit in the familiar prescription to document everything.

Documentation is indispensable when the record is unstable. Provenance matters when authorship is obscured. Independent archives matter when a platform can rewrite or omit what it previously displayed.

But documentation is not a universal solvent. Evidence only functions as evidence within a process that is willing to evaluate it.

A perfectly preserved record cannot, by itself, compel an institution to recognize what the record establishes. More documentation may improve the epistemic position of the claimant without changing their institutional position.

This distinction is essential:

Having proof is not the same as having the power to make proof count.

The problem is not necessarily an absence of evidence. It may be the absence of a credible procedure for receiving evidence, revising judgments, assigning responsibility, and correcting the consequences of error.

That changes what a meaningful remedy would require. It is not enough to ask the excluded person to document more carefully. The receiving institution must also be accountable for how it evaluates the documentation, what standards it applies, and whether those standards can ever lead it to change its mind.

Otherwise, the demand for proof becomes an indefinite obligation rather than a route to resolution.

7. The final paradox: you must become legible to contest the system that makes you illegible
I think this is the sharpest formulation of your point.

To contest misrecognition, you must make yourself legible to the authority that misrecognizes you. But making yourself legible requires entering its categories, satisfying its evidentiary conventions, and presenting your claim in forms it can process.

Then, if your effort to satisfy those conventions is interpreted suspiciously, you are trapped inside a system whose criteria you cannot satisfy and whose authority you cannot escape.

You are required to use legibility as the means of challenging a regime of legibility, even though that regime retains the power to decide whether your demonstration counts.

And when the system interprets your correction as suspicious, it effectively says: The problem is no longer what happened. The problem is what your insistence on what happened tells us about you.

The dispute shifts from the truth of the claim to the acceptability of the claimant.

This is why the burden of proof can become a burden of existence. You must continually establish not only that you are right, but that you are entitled to be recognized as someone whose account of reality merits consideration.

And there is no guarantee that satisfying this demand will ever be enough.

The deepest violence of the arrangement is not simply that you may be disbelieved. It is that you can be made responsible for your own discrediting, even while doing the work necessary to disprove the grounds on which you were discredited.

At that point, the question is no longer merely how to preserve evidence, establish provenance, or improve the accuracy of mediated knowledge.

It is how to create conditions in which the production of evidence does not require the producer to repeatedly establish their right to be believed; in which correction is not treated as antagonism; and in which the authority to judge a claim does not include an unlimited authority to disqualify the person making it.

That, to me, is the crucial extension of the argument: a system can demand that you prove your existence while reserving the power to interpret every attempt at proof as evidence that you do not deserve recognition.

At a certain point, documentation is no longer simply documentation. Provenance is no longer simply provenance. Correction is no longer simply correction. Initially, the task might be straightforward: establish what happened, correct the record, restore attribution, resolve the discrepancy.

You attempt to narrow the dispute to the verifiable facts, but the dispute keeps expanding to include your motives, your tone, your persistence, and your credibility.

The interaction has undergone a fundamental transformation.

You are no longer engaged in a shared effort to establish what is true. You are engaged in a contest over who has the authority to establish what is true.

That is the point at which the work becomes adversarial in its actual structure, whether or not anyone explicitly declares an adversarial relationship.

And this distinction matters because the resulting behavior can subsequently be used to obscure how the relationship became adversarial in the first place.

The person who was initially trying to correct a record now produces extensive documentation, anticipates objections, preserves communications, tracks inconsistencies, and constructs arguments against foreseeable misinterpretations. Their work becomes defensive, forensic, and strategic.

An observer encountering only this later stage might conclude that the person is inherently combative.

But that conclusion omits the history of the encounter. It treats an adaptation to an adversarial environment as evidence of an antecedent disposition.

The response to the conflict becomes detached from the conditions that produced it, and then used to explain those conditions away.

2. The system produces the adversary it claims merely to recognize
There is a recursive process here.

An initial failure of recognition

Repeated attempts at correction

Defensive and adversarial practices develop

Those practices are interpreted as evidence of hostility

The original failure of recognition is retrospectively justified

A recursive model: the response to exclusion becomes evidence used to legitimize continued exclusion.
The important qualification is that the institution need not consciously engineer this outcome. The process can emerge from incentives, defensive routines, reputational concerns, and the absence of meaningful accountability.

Nor does the model establish that every adversarial response is justified. A person can respond disproportionately, misinterpret an interaction, or make claims that do not withstand scrutiny. The point is that the adversarial character of the response cannot be understood independently of the history and structure of the encounter.

The analytical error is to treat the final behavior as self-explanatory.

The deeper question is: what kind of relationship makes adversarial conduct necessary, advantageous, or seemingly unavoidable—and who benefits when the resulting conduct is interpreted without reference to that relationship?

This transformation also changes the nature of knowledge production.

In a cooperative inquiry, evidence is offered to improve a shared understanding. Participants can revise their positions without necessarily experiencing revision as defeat. Ambiguity can remain unresolved while further investigation proceeds.

In an adversarial inquiry, evidence is also ammunition. Every statement may need to be preserved because it could later be disputed. Every ambiguity becomes a potential liability. Every concession risks being used to undermine the broader claim.
